meaning: Used with a negative to mean “not ... at all”. A strong, casual denial that often carries frustration or surprise.
connection: ちっとも + verb ない-form / negative adjective

senses.label: Not at all
senses.meaning: Stresses that the degree is zero: “not at all”, “not even a little”. A much stronger denial than 「あまり〜ない」.
senses.connection: ちっとも + verb ない-form (わからない／来ない／減らない)
examples: This book isn't interesting at all.
I didn't understand the teacher's explanation at all.
I'm on a diet, but my weight isn't going down at all.

senses.label: Frustration / surprise
senses.meaning: Often used to complain that things aren't going as expected. Also used to brush off someone's worry, as in 「ちっとも構わない」. More emotional than 「全然」.
senses.connection: ちっとも + 〜ない／〜ません (often with 「のに」 or 「けど」)
examples: No matter how many times I call, he never picks up.
No, I'm not tired at all.

notes: It must be followed by a negative, or the sentence falls apart: ✕「ちっとも分かった」→ ○「ちっとも分からなかった」. For a positive “a little”, use 「ちょっと」 or 「少し」.
Don't use it as if it were 「あまり」: 「あまりおいしくない」 is only “not very tasty”, while 「ちっともおいしくない」 is “not tasty at all”. Saying the latter about food someone made for you is very hurtful.
It carries obvious dissatisfaction. Saying 「ちっとも分かりません」 or 「ちっとも連絡が来ない」 to a superior or client sounds like a complaint or an accusation. At work, say 「少し分かりにくいのですが」 or 「なかなかご連絡がいただけず…」 instead.
Unlike 「全然」, it can't stand alone as an answer. Asked 「疲れた？」, you can reply 「全然。」, but you normally don't say ✕「ちっとも。」; say the full sentence 「ちっとも疲れてないよ」.

daily.title: Complaining to a friend
daily.description: Grumbling to a friend that someone or something isn't going your way.
daily.example: He never keeps his promises.

daily.title: Frustrated with practice
daily.description: A student tells their family that practice isn't paying off.
daily.example: I practice every day, but I'm not getting any better.

daily.title: Putting someone at ease
daily.description: When someone worries they're bothering you, say you don't mind at all.
daily.example: It's no trouble at all.

work.title: Chatting with a coworker
work.description: Coworkers casually complaining in private about how work is going.
work.example: This system isn't getting any easier to use, is it?

etymology: 「ちっと」 is generally thought to be an older form of 「ちょっと」 (“a little”). Adding 「も」 gives “not even a little”, and with a negative it means “not at all”.
formation: It has three parts: 「ちっと」 + 「も」 + a negative. 「ちっと」 is generally considered an older form of 「ちょっと」 and means “a tiny amount”; 「も」 is the particle meaning “even”, which singles out that minimum amount for emphasis. “Not even a little” — if even the smallest amount is denied, everything is denied, hence “not at all”. Because the structure is “not even the bare minimum”, it has to pair with a negative, and it carries a sense of disappointed expectation (“there should have been at least a little”), which is why it so often sounds like a complaint. 「少しも〜ない」 and 「一つも〜ない」 are built the same way.

similar.title: すこしも〜ない
similar.explanation: Near-synonym: both deny even the smallest amount. 「少しも」 is neutral and works in both speech and writing; 「ちっとも」 is spoken only and often sounds frustrated or complaining.

similar.title: まったく〜ない
similar.explanation: Near-synonym: the denial is just as total, but 「まったく〜ない」 sounds objective and fits formal settings (「まったく問題ありません」); 「ちっとも」 is spoken only and carries personal feeling.

similar.title: 〜ぜんぜん〜ない
similar.explanation: Near-synonym: also a total denial, but 「全然」 is more casual and can stand alone as an answer (「全然。」); 「ちっとも」 must pair with a negative and is more emotionally charged.

similar.title: 〜あまり〜ない
similar.explanation: A degree adverb it's often compared with: 「あまり〜ない」 means “not very…”, so something is still left; 「ちっとも〜ない」 means “not at all”, a degree of zero.

meaning: Used with a negative to say something happens very rarely: “rarely”, “hardly ever”.
connection: めったに + verb ない-form / めったにない + noun

senses.label: Rarely do
senses.meaning: Shows very low frequency; it almost never happens. “Rarely”, “seldom”. It only describes frequency, with no judgment from the speaker.
senses.connection: めったに + verb ない-form / 〜ません
examples: My father rarely gets angry.
It hardly ever snows around here.
I'm so busy that I rarely go to the movies these days.

senses.label: A rare ...
senses.meaning: 「めったにない」 modifies a noun directly: “a rare ...”, “a once-in-a-while ...”. Usually used for good things like chances or experiences.
senses.connection: めったにない + noun (チャンス／機会／経験)
examples: This is a rare chance.
You rarely get to see a sunset this beautiful.

notes: It must be followed by a negative: ✕「父はめったに怒る」→ ○「父はめったに怒らない」. For a positive “sometimes”, use 「たまに」: ○「たまに映画を見る」.
Mixing it up with 「全然〜ない」 changes the facts: 「父はめったに怒らない」 means “my father rarely gets angry” (he still does now and then), while 「父は全然怒らない」 means “my father never gets angry”.
「めったにない + noun」 is a positive “rare, precious…”: 「めったにないチャンス」 is “a once-in-a-lifetime chance”, not “no chance”.
「めったな〜」 used with a negative or a prohibition means “careless, reckless”, not “rare”: 「めったなことを言うな」 means “don't say anything rash”.

daily.title: Talking about habits
daily.description: Telling a friend about something you rarely do.
daily.example: I rarely cook.

daily.title: A surprise meeting
daily.description: Running into an old friend on the street after a long time.
daily.example: Fancy meeting you in a place like this. That hardly ever happens!

work.title: Encouraging someone to take a chance
work.description: A boss encourages a team member to accept an overseas posting.
work.example: A chance to work abroad doesn't come along often.

work.title: Describing a product
work.description: A shop clerk tells a customer an item is hard to get.
work.example: We rarely get this item in stock.

etymology: 「滅多」 originally meant “reckless, careless”; 「めったなことを言うな」 (“don't say rash things”) keeps that sense. With a negative it came to mean “not lightly”, and then “rarely”. The kanji 「滅多」 is generally thought to be borrowed just for the sound.
formation: 「めったに」 comes from the noun 「滅多」 (“reckless, indiscriminate”) plus the adverb-making 「に」, and originally meant “carelessly, easily”. Combined with a negative, 「めったに〜ない」 literally means “doesn't happen easily”, i.e. “rarely happens”. Because the core meaning is “easily”, it makes no sense alone in a positive sentence, so it must pair with a negative. 「めったにない + noun」 means “something you don't come by easily”, which gives the positive sense of “rare, precious”. The original sense of “careless, reckless” survives in 「めったなことを言うな」.

similar.title: 〜あまり〜ない
similar.explanation: Near-synonym: 「あまり〜ない」 can mean “not very…” for degree or frequency; 「めったに〜ない」 is only about frequency, and an even lower one — close to “hardly ever”. 「あまり行かない」 means going more often than 「めったに行かない」.

similar.title: なかなか〜ない
similar.explanation: Often confused: 「めったに〜ない」 only says something happens rarely; 「なかなか〜ない」 says something you're waiting for keeps not happening. 「このバスはめったに来ない」 = this bus line rarely runs; 「バスがなかなか来ない」 = I've been waiting ages and the bus still isn't here.

similar.title: 〜ぜんぜん〜ない
similar.explanation: Near-synonym: 「全然〜ない」 is “not at all, never”; 「めったに〜ない」 is “rarely” — it still happens once in a while.

meaning: Used with a negative to say something you want or expect is hard to achieve: “just won't ...”, “can't easily ...”.
connection: なかなか + verb ない-form / negative potential form

senses.label: Just won't ...
senses.meaning: Something you're waiting for keeps not happening: “just won't ...”, “is taking forever to ...”. Sounds impatient or helpless.
senses.connection: なかなか + verb ない-form (来ない／終わらない／治らない)
examples: The bus just won't come.
My cold just won't go away.
The meeting went on and on.

senses.label: Hard to do
senses.meaning: Even with effort, it's hard to manage: “can't seem to ...”, “not easy to ...”. Often used with the negative potential form.
senses.connection: なかなか + negative potential (覚えられない／眠れない／見つからない)
examples: I just can't remember kanji.
I have trouble falling asleep at night.
Good jobs are hard to find.

notes: Whether a negative or a positive follows changes the meaning completely: 「なかなか来ない」 is “just won't come”, while 「なかなかいい」 is “pretty good”. When listening, check whether a negative comes after it.

The positive use (「なかなか上手ですね」「なかなかおいしいですね」) carries a “better than I expected” evaluation, so using it with a superior, an elder, or a teacher sounds condescending. Say 「とてもお上手ですね」 or 「大変おいしいです」 instead.
It implies frustration that something you want just won't happen, so it can't describe mere low frequency: ✕「私はなかなかお酒を飲まない」→ ○「私はめったにお酒を飲まない」.
To state plainly that something hasn't been done yet, use 「まだ〜ていない」: 「宿題はまだ終わっていない」. Saying 「なかなか終わらない」 adds impatience or helplessness.

daily.title: Waiting for someone
daily.description: Texting a friend who's late to meet you at the station.
daily.example: You're taking forever. Where are you?

daily.title: Learning a language
daily.description: Telling your teacher your speaking isn't improving.
daily.example: My Japanese just isn't getting any better.

daily.title: Bedtime struggles
daily.description: Parents talking about a child who won't go to sleep.
daily.example: Our kid just won't go to sleep at night.

work.title: Reporting slow progress
work.description: Telling your boss the negotiations aren't moving forward.
work.example: We still haven't heard back from the client.

work.title: Hard to hire
work.description: HR discussing how hard it is to find people.
work.example: It's really hard to find experienced people, isn't it?

etymology: 「なかなか」 was originally 「中中」, meaning “in the middle, neither one thing nor the other”. From “stuck halfway, unable to finish” came the negative sense “hard to ...”. Separately, the positive sense “quite, pretty” also developed.
formation: It combines the adverb 「なかなか」 with a negative predicate. 「なかなか」 is written 「中々」; the repeated 「中」 suggests being “in the middle, neither here nor there”. With a negative, it describes something stuck halfway and unable to reach its end point, which produces “just can't…, won't… for a long time”. That's why it most often goes with verbs that have a clear end point (来る・終わる・治る) or with negative potential forms (覚えられない・眠れない). The positive sense “quite, rather” is said to have shifted from “middling” to “beyond the ordinary”. In modern Japanese the two meanings are completely separate and can only be told apart by whether a negative follows.

similar.title: 〜まだ〜ていない
similar.explanation: Near-synonym: 「まだ〜ていない」 objectively states “not yet…”; 「なかなか〜ない」 stresses that despite a long wait or real effort it still won't happen, with impatience or helplessness.

similar.title: めったに〜ない
similar.explanation: Often confused: 「めったに〜ない」 is about low frequency; 「なかなか〜ない」 is about something expected that keeps not happening. 「彼はめったに来ない」 = he rarely comes; 「彼がなかなか来ない」 = he should be here but still hasn't shown up.

similar.title: 〜(よ)うとしない
similar.explanation: Near-synonym: 「〜ようとしない」 stresses that a person “refuses” to do something — the cause is the subject's will; 「なかなか〜ない」 is usually about something being hard to achieve. 「子どもがなかなか寝ない」 may mean the child can't fall asleep; 「子どもが寝ようとしない」 means the child refuses to go to sleep.

similar.title: ちっとも〜ない
similar.explanation: Near-synonym: 「ちっとも〜ない」 stresses a degree of zero (not at all); 「なかなか〜ない」 stresses a long delay or difficulty, implying it may eventually happen.

title: 〜れる・〜られる (respectful)
meaning: Borrows the passive form to raise the person doing the action, showing respect to seniors, bosses, guests, etc. A simple kind of respectful language.
connection: Godan verb ない-stem + れる; ichidan verb + られる; する → される; 来る → 来られる

senses.label: Respecting someone's action
senses.meaning: When the subject is someone you should respect, put their action in this form to show respect. Slightly less respectful than 「お〜になる」. Very common in the news and at work.
senses.connection: 行く→行かれる／帰る→帰られる／出席する→出席される／なる→なられる
examples: The president is going to Osaka tomorrow.
The teacher has already gone home.
The department manager will attend the afternoon meeting.

senses.label: Asking the listener
senses.meaning: Used when directly asking about the listener's actions or plans. More polite than plain 「〜ますか」. A doctor's 「どうされましたか」 is a set phrase.
senses.connection: Respectful verb + ますか (飲まれますか／されますか)
examples: What would you like to drink?
What brings you in today?
Which lunch would you like?

notes: It can only describe other people's actions, never your own: ✕「私は明日大阪へ行かれます」→ ○「私は明日大阪へ参ります」. Using it about yourself is elevating yourself, which is very rude.
When speaking to people outside your company, don't use honorifics for your own boss: ✕「部長はもう帰られました」→ ○「部長の田中は本日もう退社いたしました」.
Don't stack it on other honorific forms to make a double honorific: ✕「おっしゃられる」「お帰りになられる」→ ○「おっしゃる」「お帰りになる」.

For ichidan verbs, 「〜られる」 looks identical to the potential form, which can be ambiguous: 「先生は来られますか」 can sound like both “Can you come?” and “Will you be coming?”. When asking a superior, the dedicated honorific verbs are clearer: 「いらっしゃいますか」「何を召し上がりますか」.
It also looks the same as the passive: 「先生に叱られた」 is passive (I was scolded by the teacher), while 「先生が帰られた」 is honorific. When 「〜に」 marks who did the action, it's usually passive.

daily.title: Greeting an older neighbor
daily.description: Politely asking an older neighbor where they're headed.
daily.example: Where are you off to?

daily.title: At the doctor's
daily.description: A doctor asks a patient what the problem is.
daily.example: What brings you in today?

daily.title: Watching the news
daily.description: News reports often use this form for the actions of public figures.
daily.example: The Prime Minister left for the United States this morning.

work.title: Asking about a client contact
work.description: Calling a client's office to ask when the person in charge will be back.
work.example: Around what time will Mr. Yamada be back?

work.title: Confirming a meeting
work.description: A secretary checks the boss's schedule.
work.example: Will you be attending tomorrow's meeting?

etymology: 「れる・られる」 come from the classical auxiliaries 「る・らる」, which had four uses: spontaneous, potential, passive, and respectful. They showed an action “happening naturally”, which led to a soft respect that avoids pointing directly at the other person's action.
formation: It's formed from the verb's irrealis stem (the ない-form minus 「ない」) + the auxiliary 「れる・られる」: godan verbs take 「れる」, ichidan verbs take 「られる」, and 「する」 becomes 「される」. The auxiliary comes from classical 「る・らる」, whose core meaning was “an action happening naturally, without anyone's will” (the spontaneous sense). Instead of saying outright “someone did it”, you say “the action came about naturally”, which avoids pointing directly at the person and creates a soft, indirect respect. The same “happens naturally” meaning became the passive when the subject is the one affected, and the potential when it means “can naturally be done” — which is why these uses share one form. Since it just adds an auxiliary to the verb, the structure is simple and the respect is lighter than 「お〜になる」 or the special honorific verbs.

similar.title: お〜になる
similar.explanation: Near-synonym: both are honorific. 「お〜になる」 shows more respect and can't be confused with the passive or potential; 「〜れる・られる」 is simpler and slightly less respectful, common in news and inside companies.

similar.title: いらっしゃる・おっしゃる (special honorific verbs)
similar.explanation: Near-synonym: verbs that have a dedicated honorific form (行く・来る・いる→いらっしゃる, 言う→おっしゃる, 食べる→召し上がる) should use it first. 「来られる」 and 「言われる」 are less polite and less clear than 「いらっしゃる」 and 「おっしゃる」.

similar.title: 〜れる・〜られる (passive)
similar.explanation: Same origin: it's the same auxiliary 「れる・られる」 with exactly the same forms. The passive takes the affected person as its subject and often has 「〜に」 (by whom); the honorific takes the respected person as its subject and has no agent.

similar.title: 〜られる・〜える (potential form)
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「〜られる」 on ichidan verbs also expresses ability. 「先生は来られますか」 can mean “Can you come?” or “Will you be coming?”, and only context tells which.

title: 〜のに (use)
meaning: Shows a use, purpose, or the area being evaluated: “for ...ing”, “to ...”. Followed by words like 「使う」, 「便利だ」, 「かかる」, 「必要だ」.
connection: Verb dictionary form + のに + 使う／便利だ／役に立つ／かかる／必要だ

senses.label: Used for ...
senses.meaning: Explains what something is used for, or whether it's handy for something. “Used for ...ing”, “handy for ...ing”.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + のに + 使う／便利だ／役に立つ／いい
examples: These scissors are for cutting paper.
This dictionary is handy for looking up kanji.
A smartphone is useful for finding your way.

senses.label: It takes ... to do
senses.meaning: Shows the time, money, or things needed to do something: “it takes ... to ...”, “you need ... to ...”.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + のに + 〜がかかる／〜が必要だ
examples: It cost 30 million yen to build the house.
Learning Japanese takes time.
You need a photo to get a passport.

senses.label: Good for ...
senses.meaning: Judges whether something or somewhere suits an activity. Often used with 「ちょうどいい」 or 「向いている」.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + のに + ちょうどいい／向いている／適している
examples: This park is perfect for a walk.
These shoes aren't good for walking long distances.

notes: It can't be followed by the speaker's own volitional action (go, study, buy, etc.); use 「ために」 for that: ✕「日本語を勉強するのに日本へ来ました」→ ○「日本語を勉強するために日本へ来ました」.

It looks identical to the contrastive 「のに」 (“even though”), so check the context: for purpose, the dictionary form comes before it and 「使う・便利・かかる・必要・いい」 etc. come after; when a past form comes before it and an unexpected result follows, it's contrastive. 「勉強するのにいい部屋」 is “a good room for studying”; 「勉強したのに落ちた」 is “I studied, but I still failed”.
Only the verb dictionary form can come before it; a noun takes 「に」 directly: ✕「会議のに使う」→ ○「会議に使う」; ✕「旅行のに便利」→ ○「旅行に便利」.

daily.title: Recommending something handy
daily.description: Recommending a gadget you use a lot to a friend.
daily.example: This app is great for studying English.

daily.title: Talking about your commute
daily.description: Telling a new friend how long it takes to get to work.
daily.example: It takes an hour to get to the office.

daily.title: Looking at apartments
daily.description: Commenting on a room's layout while viewing an apartment.
daily.example: This room is just right for one person, isn't it?

work.title: Explaining what a room is for
work.description: Showing a new coworker around the office.
work.example: We use this room for meetings.

work.title: Estimating a budget
work.description: Telling your boss how much a project will cost.
work.example: Building this system will take about five million yen.

etymology: Made of the nominalizer 「の」 (which turns a verb into a noun) plus the particle 「に」 for purpose or target: “for the act of ...”. It has a different origin from the conjunction 「のに」 (“even though”); they just look the same.
formation: It's built from “verb dictionary form + the nominalizer 「の」 + the particle 「に」”. 「の」 packages an action such as “cutting paper” or “looking up kanji” into a single thing (nominalization), and 「に」 marks the target or aspect, so together they mean “for doing…, when it comes to doing…”. What follows is therefore a statement about that activity: its use (使う), convenience (便利だ・いい), cost (時間がかかる), or necessity (必要だ). Because 「の」 treats the action as a general activity, it takes the tenseless dictionary form; and because it only states an aspect, it can't be followed by the speaker's volitional action — which is where it differs from 「ために」.

similar.title: 〜ために
similar.explanation: Near-synonym: both relate to purpose. 「ために」 can be followed by a volitional action (合格するために勉強する); 「のに」 can only be followed by an evaluation, use, cost, or necessity (勉強するのに便利だ).

similar.title: 〜には (purpose)
similar.explanation: Near-synonym: 「〜には」 means “in order to…, if you want to…”, usually followed by a requirement or an evaluation (合格するには努力が必要だ), with a sense of what it takes to reach a goal; 「〜のに」 focuses more on objectively describing use and cost.

similar.title: 〜ように (purpose)
similar.explanation: Near-synonym: 「ように」 also expresses purpose; it usually follows non-volitional verbs, potential forms, or negatives (忘れないようにメモする) and is followed by the action taken for it. 「のに」 can't be followed by an action — only by an evaluation or a cost.

meaning: Uses the te-form to give the reason when apologizing for doing (or not doing) something that troubled someone. It can also be thanks with a sense of apology.
connection: Verb te-form / 〜なくて / i-adjective くて + すみません

senses.label: Sorry for ...
senses.meaning: Apologizes for something you did: “Sorry for ...”, “Sorry I ...”. The te-form part gives the reason.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + すみません (遅れて／待たせて／うるさくて)
examples: Sorry I'm late.
I'm sorry to have kept you waiting.
Sorry for calling so late at night.

senses.label: Sorry for not ...
senses.meaning: Use 「〜なくて」 to apologize for not being able to do something.
senses.connection: Verb ない-form + なくて + すみません
examples: Sorry I couldn't reply.
I'm sorry I couldn't be of help.

senses.label: Sorry and thanks
senses.meaning: When someone goes out of their way for you, 「〜てもらって／てくださって すみません」 means “sorry for the trouble”: thanks mixed with apology.
senses.connection: 〜てもらって／〜てくださって + すみません
examples: Thank you for coming all this way. Sorry for the trouble.
Sorry to make you help me. Thanks.

notes: Watch the direction of the action: if you kept someone waiting, say 「お待たせしてすみません」 (causative: “I made you wait”). ✕「待ってすみません」 means “Sorry that I waited.” Likewise, worrying someone is 「ご心配をおかけしてすみません」.
「すいません」 is a casual spoken variant and isn't used in emails, documents, or formal apologies. When you've caused a superior or client real trouble, just 「すみません」 sounds flippant; say 「（大変）申し訳ございません」.
「〜てごめん」 and 「ごめんなさい」 are only for family and friends. Said to a superior, teacher, or client, they sound childish and not serious enough.
It must be connected with the te-form: ✕「遅れたすみません」→ ○「遅れてすみません」. For something you failed to do, use 「〜なくて」: ○「行けなくてすみません」.

daily.title: Late to meet a friend
daily.description: Apologizing first when you're late to meet a friend.
daily.example: Sorry to keep you waiting.

daily.title: Bothering the neighbors
daily.description: Apologizing to neighbors for the noise from home renovations.
daily.example: Sorry about the noise.

daily.title: Asking a friend for help
daily.description: Showing thanks and apology after a friend helps you move.
daily.example: Sorry to make you help on your day off.

work.title: Replying late to an email
work.description: Telling a client you're sorry for the late reply.
work.example: I'm sorry for the delay in getting back to you.

work.title: Late for a meeting
work.description: A formal apology to your boss and a client.
work.example: I sincerely apologize for being late.

etymology: 「すみません」 comes from the negative of the verb 「済む」 (“to be settled”), meaning “this can't be settled; I feel bad”. The te-form before it says “because ...”, giving the reason for the apology.
formation: It's built from “verb te-form + 「すみません」”. Here the te-form expresses a cause (“because…”), stating what you did and what it led to. 「すみません」 is the negative 「済みません」 of the verb 「済む」 (“to be settled, finished”), meaning “this can't be settled on my side; I feel bad about it”. Together they mean “because I did…, I really feel bad” — an apology for one specific thing. When someone did something for you, 「〜てくださって／〜てもらってすみません」 means “you went to trouble for me and I can't repay it”, so it doubles as thanks. Since the te-form states the cause you created, when you've put someone out you use a causative or humble form (お待たせして・ご迷惑をおかけして).

similar.title: 〜てくれてありがとう
similar.explanation: Near-synonym: both work when someone has done something for you. 「〜てくれてありがとう」 simply expresses thanks; 「〜てくださってすみません」 leans toward apologizing for the trouble you caused, and sounds humbler.

similar.title: 〜なくて (cause)
similar.explanation: It also uses the te-form to give a cause: 「〜なくて」 explains “because I didn't (couldn't)…”, and combined with 「すみません」 it becomes 「間に合わなくてすみません」 or 「お役に立てなくてすみません」, apologizing for something you failed to do.

meaning: Shows relief or satisfaction about something that already happened: “I'm glad ...”, “Good thing ...”.
connection: Verb te-form / 〜なくて / i-adjective くて / noun, na-adjective + で + よかった

senses.label: Glad I ...
senses.meaning: Looking back on something you did and feeling it was the right choice: “I'm glad I ...”.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + よかった (来て／会えて／聞いて)
examples: I'm so glad I came to Japan.
I'm really glad I met you.
I'm glad I read this book.

senses.label: Good thing ...
senses.meaning: Relief about a situation, often about avoiding something bad: “Good thing ...”, “Thank goodness ...”.
senses.connection: 〜なくて／i-adjective くて／noun, na-adjective で + よかった
examples: Good thing it didn't rain.
Thank goodness you weren't hurt.
I'm so glad everyone is safe.

senses.label: Happy for you
senses.meaning: 「〜てよかったね」 shares in someone else's good news and shows you're happy for them.
senses.connection: 〜てよかったね／〜てよかったですね
examples: You passed the exam! I'm so happy for you.
I'm glad you've recovered.

notes: It's only for things that already happened and that you're glad about. Regret over something you didn't do uses 「〜ばよかった」, which means the opposite: ✕「もっと勉強してよかった」 (when you mean regret) → ○「もっと勉強すればよかった」.

Be careful when talking about someone else's misfortune: telling someone who was injured or hit by a disaster 「〜だけでよかったですね」 (“lucky it was only…”) can come across as downplaying their loss. Show concern first: 「大変でしたね」.
For a superior's or client's good news, just 「よかったですね」 is a bit casual. On formal occasions, 「おめでとうございます」 or 「何よりです」 is more appropriate.
「よかったら」 means “if you like” and has nothing to do with 「〜てよかった」. Don't mix them up.

daily.title: Back from a trip
daily.description: Telling a friend how much you enjoyed a trip.
daily.example: I'm so glad I went to Kyoto.

daily.title: Family is safe
daily.description: Feeling relieved to hear your family is safe after an earthquake.
daily.example: Thank goodness my family is safe.

daily.title: Congratulating a friend
daily.description: Being happy for a friend who found a job.
daily.example: Great news about the job!

work.title: After a project
work.description: Coworkers looking back on a successful project.
work.example: I'm glad I got to be part of this project.

work.title: Checking with a client
work.description: Feeling relieved that a client is happy with your service.
work.example: We're glad you like it.

etymology: 「よかった」 is the past form of the adjective 「よい（いい）」. The te-form gives the reason: “because of ..., it turned out well”. That's how it expresses relief and satisfaction.
formation: It's built from “te-form + 「よかった」”. The te-form gives a cause or premise, and 「よかった」 is the past form of the adjective 「よい」; its 「た」 here evaluates a fact that has already happened. So 「〜てよかった」 means “because (it turned out that)…, the result was good” — relief or satisfaction. A negative cause uses 「〜なくて」, and nouns and na-adjectives use 「〜で」 (無事でよかった). Compare 「〜ばよかった」: 「ば」 is a hypothetical condition, “if I had done it, it would have been good”, describing something that didn't happen, so it becomes regret. The key to the meaning is whether the first part is the factual te-form or the hypothetical ば-form.

similar.title: 〜ばよかった
similar.explanation: Same origin (both built on 「よかった」) and the easiest to confuse: 「〜てよかった」 is relief about something you did; 「〜ばよかった」 is regret about something you didn't do (“I should have…”). 「来てよかった」 = I'm glad I came; 「来ればよかった」 = I wish I had come.

similar.title: 〜てくれてありがとう
similar.explanation: Near-synonym, often used in the same situations: 「来てくれてありがとう」 thanks the person directly; 「来てくれてよかった」 expresses your own relief and doesn't directly say thank you.

meaning: Means “need to ...”, “it's necessary to ...”. The negative 「必要はない」 means “there's no need to ...”.
connection: Verb dictionary form + 必要がある / noun + が必要だ

senses.label: Need to do
senses.meaning: Says that doing something is necessary: “need to ...”, “it's necessary to ...”. More objective and formal than 「〜なければならない」.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + 必要がある／必要があります
examples: You need to take the medicine every day.
You need to apply for a visa.

senses.label: Need something
senses.meaning: Says that a thing or condition is needed: “... is needed”. After a noun, use 「が必要だ」.
senses.connection: Noun + が必要だ／が必要です (〜には〜が必要だ)
examples: This job requires experience.
You need a visa to work in Japan.
A family member's signature is also needed before the surgery.

senses.label: No need to
senses.meaning: The negative means “there's no need to ...”, “you don't have to ...”. Often used to reassure someone.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + 必要はない／必要はありません
examples: There's no need to hurry.
There's no need to worry.

notes: A verb can't attach directly to 「が必要だ」: ✕「ビザを申請するが必要だ」→ ○「ビザを申請する必要がある」 or 「ビザの申請が必要だ」.
Saying 「〜する必要があります」 to a superior or client sounds like giving orders; turn it into a request instead: ✕「部長も確認する必要があります」→ ○「部長にもご確認いただけますでしょうか」.
「〜必要はない」 sounds objective and can come across as cold: telling a client 「来る必要はありません」 sounds like a rejection. Say 「お越しいただかなくても大丈夫です」 instead.
The negative normally uses 「は」: 「心配する必要はない」 sounds more natural than 「必要がない」.

daily.title: Getting ready for a trip
daily.description: A friend asks what they need for a trip abroad.
daily.example: You need a passport to travel abroad.

daily.title: Reassuring someone
daily.description: Comforting a friend who wants to apologize for something small.
daily.example: There's no need to apologize.

work.title: In a meeting
work.description: Pointing out something that needs to improve.
work.example: We need to rethink this approach.

work.title: Job requirements
work.description: A job ad stating the requirements.
work.example: Applicants need JLPT N2 or higher.

etymology: 「必要」 is a word borrowed from Chinese, meaning “must have, indispensable”. In Japanese it works as a noun and a na-adjective, and combines with 「ある」 or 「だ」 to form this pattern.
formation: The core is the Sino-Japanese noun 「必要」 (“necessity”). 「〜必要がある」 is “verb dictionary form directly modifying the noun 「必要」 + 「が」 + the existence verb 「ある」”, literally “there exists a need to do…”, so nothing like 「が」 or 「の」 goes between the verb and 「必要」. 「〜が必要だ」, on the other hand, uses 「必要」 as a na-adjective predicate, “N is necessary”, so only a noun (or 「〜こと」) can come before it. In the negative, 「は」 makes “need” the focus of contrast and negates it, giving 「必要はない」 (“need — there is none”), which is why it sounds more natural than 「必要がない」.

similar.title: 〜なければならない
similar.explanation: Near-synonym: 「〜なければならない」 carries a sense of duty, “have to”; 「〜必要がある」 objectively states that doing it is necessary, and is more common in explanatory texts and notices.

similar.title: 〜ないといけない
similar.explanation: Near-synonym: 「〜ないといけない」 is the conversational “gotta…”; 「〜必要がある」 is more written and objective, and better suited to formal settings.

similar.title: 〜なくてもいい
similar.explanation: Close in meaning to the negative 「必要はない」: 「〜なくてもいい」 means “you don't have to…” and is more casual and gentle; 「〜必要はない」 means “there's no need to…” and is more objective and blunt.

similar.title: 〜べきだ
similar.explanation: Near-synonym: 「べきだ」 is the speaker's subjective view that one “should…”, with a moral judgment; 「必要がある」 only states an objective need.

title: 〜自動詞・他動詞 (intransitive/transitive pairs)
meaning: Pairs of intransitive and transitive verbs. Intransitive verbs describe a thing changing by itself (〜が); transitive verbs describe a person changing it on purpose (〜を).
connection: Noun + が + intransitive verb (開く) / noun + を + transitive verb (開ける)

senses.label: Intransitive verbs
senses.meaning: Describe a thing's own change or state, without caring who did it. The particle is 「が」. Like “(the door) opened”.
senses.connection: Nが + 開く／閉まる／始まる／消える／壊れる／落ちる
examples: The door blew open in the wind.
Class starts at nine.
Suddenly the lights went out.

senses.label: Transitive verbs
senses.meaning: Describe a person doing something to a thing on purpose. The particle is 「を」. Like “(someone) opened the door”.
senses.connection: Nを + 開ける／閉める／始める／消す／壊す／落とす
examples: Please open the window.
Well then, let's begin the meeting.
I turned off the lights before going out.

senses.label: Describing states
senses.meaning: Intransitive + ている shows the resulting state after a change. Transitive + てある shows a state someone set up on purpose.
senses.connection: Nが + intransitive ている / Nが + transitive てある
examples: The window is open.
The window has been opened (by someone).

senses.label: Taking responsibility
senses.meaning: An intransitive verb says something “just happened”, so it doesn't stress responsibility. A transitive verb says you did it and owns the responsibility. Apologies sound more sincere with a transitive verb.
senses.connection: Nが + intransitive (割れた) / Nを + transitive (割ってしまった)
examples: Oh, the glass broke.
I'm sorry, I broke a plate.

notes: Match the particle to the verb: intransitive verbs take 「が」, transitive verbs take 「を」. ✕「電気を消えた」→ ○「電気が消えた／電気を消した」; ✕「会議を始まります」→ ○「会議を始めます」.

In Japan, if you broke or lost something yourself, using an intransitive verb (「コップが割れました」「財布がなくなりました」) sounds like dodging responsibility. When apologizing, use the transitive verb to admit you did it: 「コップを割ってしまいました」.
「〜てある」 only attaches to transitive verbs: ✕「窓が開いてある」→ ○「窓が開けてある」 (someone left it open on purpose) / 「窓が開いている」 (it's open).
A transitive verb + 「〜ている」 usually means the action is in progress: 「ドアを開けている」 is “(someone) is opening the door”, not “the door is open”.

daily.title: At home
daily.description: A family member reminds you to turn off the light.
daily.example: The light's still on. Turn it off.

daily.title: Something broke
daily.description: A child tells their parents a toy broke. The intransitive verb makes it sound unintentional.
daily.example: My toy broke.

daily.title: Checking before leaving
daily.description: Checking the doors and windows before going out.
daily.example: Did you lock the door properly?

work.title: Opening a meeting
work.description: The chair announces the start of the meeting with a transitive verb.
work.example: Well then, let's begin the meeting.

work.title: Preparing the venue
work.description: Confirming that the meeting room is ready.
work.example: The handouts are already laid out on the desks.

etymology: Japanese intransitive and transitive verbs are often formed from the same root with different endings, like 「あく／あける」 and 「こわれる／こわす」. These pairs are thought to go back to ancient times. The terms 「自動詞」 and 「他動詞」 were brought in from Western grammar in the modern era.
formation: Most intransitive/transitive pairs share one root with different endings: the root carries “what changes”, and the ending decides whether it “changes by itself” or “is made to change”. Common patterns: verbs with 「-ar-」 are usually intransitive (始まる・上がる) and pair with transitive verbs with 「-e-」 (始める・上げる); intransitive verbs with 「-e-」 (壊れる・消える) pair with transitive verbs with 「-s-」 (壊す・消す). The 「す」 in transitive endings is generally thought to be related to an old causative 「す」, which is why verbs with 「す」 usually mean “make something…”. The subject of an intransitive verb is the thing that changes, marked with 「が」; a transitive verb needs a doer who treats the thing as an object, marked with 「を」. Remember “same root, ending decides intransitive or transitive”, and you can learn and guess the verbs in pairs.

similar.title: 〜てある
similar.explanation: Near-synonym: a transitive verb + 「てある」 and an intransitive verb + 「ている」 both describe a resulting state. 「窓が開けてある」 implies someone did it on purpose; 「窓が開いている」 just describes the state.

similar.title: 〜せる・〜させる (causative)
similar.explanation: Near-synonym: both mean “make something change”. When there's no matching transitive verb, or you mean “have someone do it themselves”, use the causative: 「子どもを起こす」 (wake the child up) vs. 「子どもを立たせる」 (make the child stand up).

similar.title: 〜れる・〜られる (passive)
similar.explanation: Near-synonym: the passive can also leave out the doer, but it still implies “someone did it” (窓が開けられた); an intransitive verb describes the thing changing by itself (窓が開いた).

meaning: A judgment based on appearance: “looks ...”, “seems ...”. The reality may be different.
connection: i-adjective stem + く見える / na-adjective, noun + に見える

senses.label: Looks (i-adjectives)
senses.meaning: Describes the impression something gives from the outside: “looks ...”. Often hints that the reality is different.
senses.connection: i-adjective stem + く見える (若く／おいしく／大きく)
examples: My mother looks younger than she is.
This cake looks really delicious.
That outfit makes you look grown-up.

senses.label: Looks (na-adjectives, nouns)
senses.meaning: With a na-adjective or noun: “looks ...”, “looks like a ...”.
senses.connection: na-adjective + に見える / noun + に見える
examples: She always looks full of energy.
That person looks like a student.
This dish looks easy, but it's actually hard.

senses.label: Doesn't look ...
senses.meaning: The negative 「〜には見えない」 means “doesn't look ...”. Often used as a compliment, e.g. on looking young.
senses.connection: Noun, na-adjective + には見えない / i-adjective く + は見えない
examples: You don't look 60 at all.
He doesn't look that busy.

notes: I-adjectives change to 「く」; nouns and na-adjectives take 「に」, with no 「の」 after a noun: ✕「おいしいに見える」→ ○「おいしく見える」; ✕「学生のに見える」→ ○「学生に見える」. Verbs and whole sentences need 「〜ように見える」.

「〜く／に見える」 only describes outward impression and often hints “but it may not really be so”. When praising food someone made, people usually say 「おいしそう！」; 「おいしく見える」 can sound like “it only looks tasty”.

Be careful when commenting on someone's age or looks: 「〜歳に見えます」 is very rude if the age is higher than their real one. To say someone looks young, 「お若いですね」 is common; 「若く見えますね」 can be taken as “you're not actually young”.
The 「見える」 in 「海が見える」 or 「遠くに山が見える」 means “can be seen”, not “looks”: 「遠くに見える」 means “visible in the distance”, not “looks far away”.

daily.title: Complimenting a friend
daily.description: A friend has a new hairstyle and you say it makes her look young.
daily.example: That hairstyle makes you look younger.

daily.title: Shopping online
daily.description: Comparing clothes you bought online with the photo.
daily.example: It looked so much more expensive in the photo.

daily.title: Meeting a friend's child
daily.description: Surprised at how grown-up a friend's son looks.
daily.example: Your son already looks like a college student.

work.title: Reviewing a design
work.description: Commenting on a poster in a design meeting.
work.example: With this color, the text looks small.

work.title: Checking on a coworker
work.description: A coworker looks unwell and you ask how they are.
work.example: You look a little pale. Are you OK?

etymology: 「見える」 is the spontaneous form of 「見る」, originally “to come into view naturally”. After state forms like 「〜く」 or 「〜に」, it came to mean “to appear as ...”, that is, “to look ...”.
formation: It's built from “the adverbial form of an adjective (i-adjective 「〜く」 / na-adjective or noun 「〜に」) + 「見える」”. 「く」 and 「に」 mean “appearing in the state of…”, the same as in 「若くなる」 and 「静かになる」. 「見える」 is the spontaneous form of 「見る」, meaning “to come into view naturally”, and its subject is the thing being seen. So 「若く見える」 literally means “comes into view looking young”. Because the viewer usually isn't mentioned and the judgment comes only from appearance, it often implies “not necessarily in reality”. Verbs and sentences have no 「く／に」 form, so they connect to 「見える」 through 「〜ように」.

similar.title: 〜ように見える
similar.explanation: Same origin, near-synonym: 「〜ように見える」 can attach to verbs and whole sentences (怒っているように見える) and carries a guess; 「〜く／に見える」 mainly attaches to adjectives and nouns and directly describes appearance.

similar.title: 〜そうだ (appearance)
similar.explanation: Near-synonym: 「おいしそうだ」 guesses an inner quality from appearance and is the usual way to compliment; 「おいしく見える」 focuses on the impression the appearance gives, sometimes implying “not necessarily in reality”.

similar.title: 〜とみえる
similar.explanation: Same origin (both use 「見える」): 「〜とみえる」 follows a sentence and infers from signs, “it seems that…” (よほど疲れていたとみえる), and is more written; 「〜く／に見える」 describes appearance.

similar.title: 〜が見える・〜が聞こえる
similar.explanation: Same origin: the basic meaning of 「見える」, “can be seen”. 「山が見える」 means you can see the mountains; only with 「く／に」 describing a state before it does it mean “looks…”.

meaning: After a number + counter, shows an interval in time or space: “every ...”, “every other ...”.
connection: Number + counter + おきに / おきの + noun

senses.label: Time intervals
senses.meaning: Something repeats at regular intervals. With 「日」, 「一日おき」 means “every other day”. With 「分」 or 「時間」, 「10分おき」 usually just means “every 10 minutes”.
senses.connection: Number + 日／週間／時間／分 + おきに
examples: This bus comes every 15 minutes.
Please take the medicine every 6 hours.
My mother goes to the gym every other day.

senses.label: Space intervals
senses.meaning: Things are arranged at regular distances or counts.
senses.connection: Number + メートル／行／駅／人 + おきに
examples: Trees are planted every 10 meters along the road.
Please write on every other line in your notebook.

senses.label: Modifying nouns
senses.meaning: 「〜おきの + noun」 modifies a noun: “a ... every ...”.
senses.connection: Number + counter + おきの + noun
examples: You need a break every hour.
I've gotten used to working every third day.

notes: 「1日おき」 means “every other day” (the 1st, 3rd, 5th…), not “every day”; 「2日おきに」 means once every three days. Mishear this in a doctor's instructions or a shift schedule and the count is completely wrong.

With units like 「日・週・年・人」, 「3日おき」 and 「3日ごとに」 can differ by one unit, and even Japanese speakers often interpret them differently. For important things like medication or shift changes, confirm with specific dates or 「〜日に1回」.
It must follow a “number + unit”: ✕「月曜日おきに」→ ○「1週間おきの月曜日に」 / 「隔週の月曜日に」.

daily.title: Taking the train
daily.description: A friend asks how often the trains come.
daily.example: The trains come every 5 minutes, so no need to rush.

daily.title: Looking after plants
daily.description: Telling your family how often to water the flowers.
daily.example: Water this flower every other day, OK?

daily.title: After seeing the doctor
daily.description: A pharmacist explains how to take the medicine.
daily.example: Please take one tablet every 4 hours.

work.title: Factory inspections
work.description: Explaining how often the machines are checked.
work.example: We inspect the machines every two hours.

work.title: Setting up a venue
work.description: Arranging the spacing of the chairs.
work.example: Please place the chairs one meter apart.

etymology: 「おき」 comes from the continuative form of the verb 「置く」, which can mean “to leave a gap” (as in 「間を置く」). 「一日おき」 originally meant “leaving one day open”, which gives the sense of “every other”.
formation: It's built from “number + unit + 「おき」 + 「に／の」”. 「おき」 is the masu-stem of the verb 「置く」 used as a noun, and 「置く」 can mean “leave a gap, space out” (「間を置く」「一行置いて書く」). 「1日おき」 literally means “leaving 1 day empty”: you do it once, skip 1 day, then do it again — so every other day, once every two days. 「に」 makes it an adverb modifying an action, and 「の」 lets it modify a noun. With continuous quantities like minutes or meters, “leaving 15 minutes” and “every 15 minutes” amount to the same thing, so it means the same as 「ごとに」.

similar.title: 〜ごとに
similar.explanation: Near-synonym: 「ごとに」 means “once every…”, so 「3日ごとに」 is once every three days; 「おきに」 stresses “leaving a gap”. With continuous units like minutes or meters they're the same, but with days or people they can differ by one unit.

similar.title: 〜たびに
similar.explanation: Near-synonym: 「たびに」 attaches to actions or events and means “every time…” (会うたびに); 「おきに」 attaches to quantities and means a fixed interval.

similar.title: 〜ておく
similar.explanation: Same origin (both from 「置く」): 「〜ておく」 “puts down” the result of an action (doing it in advance, leaving it as is); 「おき」 takes the “leave a gap, space out” sense of 「置く」.

meaning: Attached to certain feeling or sensation adjectives to make a noun meaning “a person who easily feels ...”, like 「寒がり」 (“someone who feels the cold easily”).
connection: Adjective stem + がり (屋) / verb ます-stem + たがり (屋)

senses.label: Someone who easily feels ...
senses.meaning: Someone who naturally tends to feel a certain way: “sensitive to ...”, “easily ...”. Works as a noun or a na-adjective.
senses.connection: 寒がり・暑がり・怖がり・痛がり／恥ずかしがり屋・寂しがり屋
examples: I really feel the cold, so I don't like winter.
My little sister scares easily, so she doesn't watch horror movies.
Our child is shy and can't talk to strangers.

senses.label: Someone who always wants to ...
senses.meaning: 「〜たがり（屋）」 means “someone who always wants to ...”, often with mild criticism.
senses.connection: Verb ます-stem + たがり (屋) (目立ちたがり屋／知りたがり)
examples: He's a show-off.
Our child is so curious, always asking questions every day.

senses.label: Putting on a brave face
senses.meaning: 「強がり」 is a fixed noun meaning “bravado, acting tough”. It's not a type of person.
senses.connection: 強がり (を言う)
examples: He said “I'm fine,” but he was just acting tough.

notes: 「〜がり屋」 and 「〜たがり屋」 often sound critical: calling someone 「目立ちたがり屋」 or 「知りたがり」 to their face — especially a superior or an elder — is quite rude. Saying it about yourself is fine (「私、寒がりなんです」).
「寒がり」 is a lasting personality trait, not a feeling right now: ✕「今日は寒がりです」→ ○「今日は寒いです」. For how someone is acting at the moment, use 「寒がっている」.
「強がり」 means “putting on a brave front”, not “a strong person”; 「怖がり」 means “a scaredy-cat”, not “a scary person”.
It's limited to a small set of fixed words (寒い・暑い・怖い・痛い・恥ずかしい・寂しい, etc.) and can't be extended freely: ✕「おいしがり」.

daily.title: Talking about yourself
daily.description: Telling a friend about your constitution.
daily.example: I really feel the cold.

daily.title: Introducing your family
daily.description: Explaining to a guest that your child is shy with strangers.
daily.example: This one is a bit shy.

daily.title: In a novel
daily.description: A novel describes a character's personality.
daily.example: She got lonely easily and didn't like being by herself.

work.title: Adjusting the AC
work.description: Explaining to coworkers that you feel the cold and asking them to turn up the temperature.
work.example: I get cold easily. Would it be OK to turn up the AC a little?

etymology: 「〜がり」 is the noun made from the continuative form of the suffix 「〜がる」 (“to show signs of ...”), and 「屋」 means “that kind of person”. “Always showing signs of ...” came to mean a person with that tendency.
formation: It's built from “adjective stem + the suffix 「がる」 → its masu-stem used as a noun, 「がり」 (+ 「屋」)”. 「がる」 means “to show a feeling outwardly”, so 「寒がる」 is “to act cold”; as the noun 「寒がり」 it means “a person or personality that always acts cold”. 「屋」 originally meant a shop or someone in a trade, and was extended to “a person with a certain character” (がんばり屋・気分屋); adding it stresses “that's just the kind of person they are”. 「たがり」 is 「た」, the stem of 「たい」, + 「がる」: “a person who always shows they want to do…”. Since 「がる」 describes a visible outward tendency, 「〜がり」 refers to a lasting personality, not a feeling at the moment.

similar.title: 〜がる・〜がっている
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「〜がる」 is a verb describing how someone else is acting right now (弟が寒がっている); 「〜がり」 is its noun form and refers to a person's general tendency (弟は寒がりだ).

similar.title: 〜たがる
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「〜たがる」 describes someone else wanting to do something (行きたがっている); 「〜たがり（屋）」 refers to a person who always wants to do something (目立ちたがり屋).

similar.title: 〜っぽい
similar.explanation: Near-synonym: 「忘れっぽい」 and 「怒りっぽい」 also describe a tendency, “prone to…”, but 「っぽい」 makes an adjective and attaches to a verb's masu-stem or a noun; 「〜がり」 is a noun and mainly attaches to adjectives of feeling.

meaning: Quotes information you heard from someone else: “I heard that ...”. It makes clear the source is hearsay.
connection: Plain form + と聞いた／と聞きました／と聞いている (casual: 〜って聞いた)

senses.label: I heard
senses.meaning: Passes on news you heard from someone: “I heard that ...”. The source can be marked with 「〜から」 or 「〜に」.
senses.connection: Plain form + と聞いた／と聞きました／って聞いた
examples: I heard Mr. Tanaka is getting married next month.
I heard the ramen at that place is good.
A friend told me it's going to rain tomorrow.

senses.label: What I've been told
senses.meaning: 「〜と聞いている」 means “I've been told that ...”, “as far as I know ...”. It treats what you heard as a known premise and sounds fairly formal. The humble form is 「〜と伺っております」.
senses.connection: Plain form + と聞いている／と聞いております／と伺っております
examples: I was told the meeting starts at 3.
We understand that Mr. Yamada will be visiting today.

senses.label: On hearing ...
senses.meaning: 「〜と聞いて」 shows your reaction or feeling after hearing some news: “When I heard ..., I felt ...”.
senses.connection: Plain form + と聞いて + 安心した／驚いた／うれしかった
examples: I was relieved to hear you passed.
I was shocked to hear there'd been an accident.

notes: 「聞く」 also means “to ask”, and when what comes before it is a question the meaning changes completely: 「先生に試験はいつかと聞いた」 is “I asked the teacher when the exam is”; only 「試験は来週だと聞いた」 is “I heard”.
Marking the source with 「から」 is clearer: 「友達から聞いた」 means “I heard it from a friend”, while 「友達に聞いた」 could also be understood as “I asked a friend”.
When passing something on to a superior or client, 「〜と聞きました」 is a bit casual; use the humble 「〜と伺いました」 or 「〜と伺っております」.
「伺う」 shows respect to the person who said it, so you can't use it when relaying your own boss's words to a client: ✕「社長から〜と伺っております」→ ○「社長の田中から〜と聞いております」.

daily.title: Gossiping
daily.description: Friends sharing news they heard.
daily.example: Did you hear Sato quit his job?

daily.title: Recommending a place
daily.description: Passing on someone else's recommendation to a friend.
daily.example: I heard a new café opened in front of the station.

daily.title: Checking on a friend
daily.description: Sending a message after hearing a friend is sick.
daily.example: I was worried when I heard you were in the hospital.

work.title: Confirming details
work.description: Confirming with a client something you heard earlier.
work.example: I understand you'll be on a business trip from next week. When will you be back?

work.title: Handing over work
work.description: Telling the new person in charge what you know.
work.example: I was told the deadline is the end of the month.

etymology: 「聞く」 originally means “to hear”, and later also “to ask”. The particle 「と」 marks the quoted content, so 「〜と聞く」 means “to hear (something) like ...”.
formation: It's built from “quoted content + the particle 「と」 + 「聞く」”. 「と」 marks what is quoted, so 「〜と聞く」 literally means “to hear the words ‘…’”. The subject is the listener (usually me), so the focus is “this is something I heard — secondhand information”. With 「た」 it's a one-time fact of hearing; with 「ている」 it's “being in the state of having heard”, which is why in business 「〜と聞いております」 means “information we've been told”. 「〜と聞いて + emotion」 uses the te-form for a cause: “when I heard…, I felt…”. Since 「聞く」 also means “to ask”, when a question (〜か) comes before it, it becomes “asked”.

similar.title: 〜そうだ (hearsay)
similar.explanation: Near-synonym: 「〜そうだ」 just passes on the information and is more objective; 「〜と聞いた」 highlights “I heard” and can name the source (友達から〜と聞いた).

similar.title: 〜と言っていた (reporting)
similar.explanation: Near-synonym: 「〜と言っていた」 takes the speaker as its subject (田中さんが〜と言っていた); 「〜と聞いた」 takes the listener (me) as its subject — two angles on the same event.

similar.title: 〜んだって
similar.explanation: Near-synonym: 「〜んだって」 is conversational hearsay (明日休みなんだって), mostly between friends; 「〜と聞いた」 is neutral and, with 「ました」, works in formal settings.

similar.title: 〜によると・〜によれば
similar.explanation: Near-synonym: 「〜によると」 explicitly names the source and often pairs with 「〜そうだ」, and is more written (ニュースによると〜そうだ); 「〜と聞いた」 is more conversational.

meaning: Shows a common saying or legend: “it is said that ...”, “people generally believe ...”. It doesn't name a specific speaker.
connection: Plain form + と言われている / と言われる + noun

senses.label: It is said / widely believed
senses.meaning: Passes on a widely held view, common knowledge, or legend: “it is said that ...”, “it's generally thought that ...”. The speaker doesn't take responsibility for it.
senses.connection: Plain form + と言われている／と言われています／と言われてきた
examples: This temple is said to be the oldest in Japan.
Walking 10,000 steps a day is said to be good for your health.
Since long ago, people have said a dragon lives in this lake.

senses.label: Said to be ...
senses.meaning: 「〜と言われる + noun」 modifies a noun: “a ... said to be ...”, “the so-called ...”.
senses.connection: Plain form + と言われる + noun
examples: I tried what's said to be the best coffee in the world.
This is a shrine said to make love come true.

notes: 「〜と言われている」 means “it's widely said”, with no specific speaker; 「（医者に）〜と言われた」 means “someone told me…”, often with a sense of being warned or criticized: 「医者にお酒をやめろと言われた」. Don't mix them up.
It presents a circulating claim, not a proven fact. Using it as solid evidence in a report or paper invites criticism; when you need a source, use 「〜によると」 and cite it.
Reporting a superior's instruction as 「部長に〜と言われました」 often sounds passive and reluctant. In a formal report, say 「部長から〜とのご指示がありました」.

daily.title: Sightseeing
daily.description: A tour guide tells visitors a legend about a sight.
daily.example: This tree is said to be over a thousand years old.

daily.title: Talking about health
daily.description: Friends discussing everyday health tips.
daily.example: They say if you skip breakfast, you gain weight more easily.

daily.title: Watching the news
daily.description: A TV news report explains the cause of something.
daily.example: Global warming is said to be the cause.

work.title: Citing a common view in a report
work.description: Quoting a widely held view in the industry.
work.example: This market is expected to keep growing.

work.title: Presenting a product
work.description: A salesperson highlights a product's selling point.
work.example: This material is said to be gentle on the skin.

etymology: Made of 「言われる」 (the passive of 「言う」) plus 「ている」. “Being said (by everyone)” means “this has long been said”, so it expresses a common view or legend.
formation: It's built from “quotative 「と」 + 「言われる」, the passive of 「言う」, + 「ている」”. Using the passive without naming a speaker shows the speaker is “people in general”, so it expresses common opinion or legend. 「ている」 shows the state continues — “it keeps being said” — i.e. it's widely held; 「〜と言われてきた」 stresses it has been handed down from the past. 「〜と言われる + noun」 modifies a noun: “the … that is called …”. Because the speaker hides behind it and doesn't take responsibility for the content, the tone is objective and leaves room for doubt, which suits news and explanatory writing.

similar.title: 〜とされている
similar.explanation: Near-synonym: 「〜とされている」 is more written and formal, common in academic and official documents; 「〜と言われている」 works in both speech and writing.

similar.title: 〜と考えられている
similar.explanation: Near-synonym with the same structure (quote + passive + ている): 「〜と考えられている」 focuses on an inference or view with some basis; 「〜と言われている」 focuses on the circulating claim itself.

similar.title: 〜そうだ (hearsay)
similar.explanation: Near-synonym: 「〜そうだ」 usually relays a specific piece of news you heard once; 「〜と言われている」 refers to something said widely over a long time.

similar.title: 〜ということだ (hearsay / conclusion)
similar.explanation: Near-synonym: 「〜ということだ」 also expresses hearsay, usually relaying specific information, and is more written (明日は休講だということだ); 「〜と言われている」 is what society commonly says.

meaning: The speaker thinks a certain description is fair: “you could say ...”, “it's no exaggeration to say ...”. A softened assertion.
connection: Noun / plain form + と言ってもいい (だろう)

senses.label: You could say
senses.meaning: “It's not 100% true, but it's fair to say so.” Softer than stating it outright. Often followed by 「でしょう」 or 「だろう」.
senses.connection: Noun (だ) / plain form + と言ってもいい／と言ってもいいでしょう
examples: You could say this movie is the best of the year.
You could say he's the face of this shop.
You could say smartphones are part of the modern body.

senses.label: Almost
senses.meaning: 「〜と言ってもいいくらい／ほど」 shows a high degree: “so much that you could almost say ...”.
senses.connection: Noun / plain form + と言ってもいいくらい／ほど
examples: I come here almost every day.
Her Japanese is practically perfect.

senses.label: No exaggeration
senses.meaning: The strong form 「〜と言っても過言ではない／言い過ぎではない」 means “it's no exaggeration to say ...”. Stronger and more formal.
senses.connection: Noun / plain form + と言っても過言ではない
examples: It's no exaggeration to call this a historic discovery.
It's no overstatement to say he saved the company.

notes: Add 「か」 at the end and it becomes a request for permission: 「〜と言ってもいいですか」 means “May I say…?”, not “It could be said that…”.
Drop 「いい」 and the meaning changes a lot: 「〜といっても」 is “although it's called… (it's not really that much)”, so 「社長といっても社員は3人だけだ」 is belittling; 「彼はこの会社の顔と言ってもいい」 is a positive evaluation.

It's the tone of the speaker passing judgment. Using it to evaluate a superior's or elder's ability to their face (✕「部長の判断は正しいと言ってもいいです」) can sound like you're grading them. For direct praise, say 「さすがです」 or 「勉強になります」.

daily.title: Praising a friend's cooking
daily.description: Complimenting a friend after eating their food.
daily.example: This is basically restaurant quality!

daily.title: Talking about your hometown
daily.description: Telling a friend about a local specialty.
daily.example: You could say this tea is my town's pride.

daily.title: Reading a review
daily.description: A film review assesses a director's work.
daily.example: This is arguably the director's masterpiece.

work.title: Reporting project results
work.description: Summing up a project's success in a meeting.
work.example: You could say this success is the result of the whole team's hard work.

work.title: Assessing market position
work.description: An analysis report describes a product's position.
work.example: It's no exaggeration to call this product the industry standard.

etymology: Made of the quoting 「と」 + the te-form of 「言う」 + 「〜てもいい」 (permission). Literally “it's OK even if you say ...”. From permission it shifted to a soft judgment by the speaker.
formation: It's built from “quotative 「と」 + 「言って」, the te-form of 「言う」, + 「も」 + 「いい」” — that is, 「と言う」 plus the permission pattern 「〜てもいい」. Literally it means “even if you call it ‘…’, that's fine (it's not wrong)”. By saying “it's okay to put it this way”, the speaker accepts the evaluation while leaving some room, so it becomes a soft assertion. Swap 「いい」 for the stronger 「過言ではない」 (“not an exaggeration”) and you get the stronger 「〜と言っても過言ではない」; drop 「いい」, and 「と言っても」 keeps only the concessive “even if you say…”, giving 「〜といっても」.

similar.title: 〜と言える
similar.explanation: Near-synonym: 「〜と言える」 means “it can be said that…”, a more objective, well-founded judgment; 「〜と言ってもいい」 is softer, with a sense of “it's no stretch to say”.

similar.title: 〜と言っても過言ではない
similar.explanation: Near-synonym, same origin: 「〜と言っても過言ではない」 means “it's no exaggeration to say…”, a stronger assertion and more written; 「〜と言ってもいい」 is milder and works in speech too.

similar.title: 〜といっても
similar.explanation: Same origin (both from 「と言っても」): 「〜といっても」 means “although it's called… (it's not really that much)”, a concession; 「〜と言ってもいい」 ends in 「いい」 and affirms an evaluation.

similar.title: 〜てもいい
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「〜てもいい」 basically grants permission; 「〜と言ってもいい」 means “it's fine to call it…” and has become fixed as the speaker's soft judgment, no longer expressing permission.
